title: Enuma Elish, Tablet IV: Marduk defeats Tiamat
source: British Museum tablet photographs + eBL manuscript transliterations (eBL corpus edition L I.2, Poem of Creation (Enuma elish) (ed. A. C. Heinrich, rev. Z. J. Földi and E. Jiménez), SB IV) + English of the eBL edition (B. R. Foster (eBL edition))
description: Enuma Elish (the Babylonian Poem of Creation), Tablet IV: 141 of 146 lines, each shown on a photographed cuneiform tablet (11 tablets), with the eBL transliteration of that tablet and B. R. Foster's English translation.
introduction:
The gods give Marduk kingship and weapons. He rides out on his storm chariot, catches Tiamat in his net, kills her with an arrow, binds her helpers and Qingu, takes the Tablet of Destinies, and splits Tiamat's body in two to form the sky.

Enuma Elish ('When on high'), the Babylonian Poem of Creation, tells how Marduk, god of Babylon, defeated Tiamat, created the ordered world and became king of the gods. It was written on seven tablets and recited in Babylon during the New Year festival. The date of composition is debated (proposals range from the 18th to the 12th century BCE); the surviving copies date from the 9th to the 2nd century BCE and come from Ashur, Nineveh, Kish, Babylon, Sippar, Uruk and other sites. This page follows the line numbering of the electronic Babylonian Library edition.

How this page is built. Each section is a run of consecutive lines as written on one photographed clay tablet. For every line the eBL edition (https://www.ebl.lmu.de/corpus/L/1/2/SB/IV) lists the manuscripts that carry it, with each tablet's own column and line numbers; the tablet chosen for each run is the photographed manuscript with the most signs preserved there. The original text is eBL's transliteration of that tablet's signs (not a modern composite text): square brackets mark broken signs, x an illegible sign, # a damaged sign, ? an uncertain reading, and words in {braces} are determinatives. Superscript numbers are the line numbers of the eBL edition, used in both the Akkadian and the English. The English is B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), one line of English per line of the poem; italics mark uncertain renderings, as in the source.

Finding a line on the photograph. Each section names the tablet, the face and column, and the tablet's own line numbers (a prime, as in 5', counts from the first preserved line of a broken column). On a tablet with six columns the obverse carries columns i-iii from left to right; the reverse, turned over from bottom to top, carries columns iv-vi from right to left. The photographs often show the obverse above the reverse with the edges around them; a fragment preserves only part of this layout.

This page shows 141 of the 146 lines of the eBL edition (97%), from 11 tablets in the British Museum: BM.33891, K.1353 (Nineveh), BM.36667, K.16706 (Nineveh), K.7361 (Nineveh), F.2, BM.36387, K.3437 (Nineveh), K.5420.C (Nineveh), K.4657 (Nineveh), K.11863 (Nineveh).

Lines not shown. 5 of the 146 lines of the eBL edition have no witness here with an open photograph: 25 (only on VAT.10552, SU-1951.58, SU-1951.47, BM.93016); 130 (only on SU-1951.58, SU-1951.47, SU-1952.243, BM.93016); 133-135 (only on SU-1951.58, SU-1951.47, SU-1952.243, BM.93016). Lines that survive only on tablets whose photographs are not openly licensed (for example in the Iraq Museum, Berlin, Istanbul, Ankara, Philadelphia or private collections), or only on tablets whose eBL photograph does not show the lines, are omitted.
translator_notes: Akkadian: eBL transliteration of the signs on the photographed tablet (manuscript-level ATF), not a composite text.
English: B. R. Foster's translation in the eBL edition; it renders eBL's composite text, including restorations from other tablets.
Line numbers: eBL edition. Each section also gives the tablet's own column and line numbers.

translation.text:
37He took up a mace, held it in his right hand,
38Bow and quiver he slung at his side.
39Thunderbolts he set before his face,
40With raging fire he covered his body.
41Then he made a net to enclose Tiamat within it,
42He deployed the four winds that none of her might escape:
43South Wind, North Wind, East Wind, West Wind,
44He fastened the net at his side, gift of his grandfather Anu;
45He made ill wind, whirlwind, cyclone,
46Four-ways wind, seven-ways wind, destructive wind, back-and-forth wind:
47He released the winds that he had made, the seven of them,
48Mounting in readiness behind him to roil inside Tiamat.
49Then the Lord raised the Deluge, his great weapon.
50He mounted the terrible chariot, the unopposable Storm Demon,
51He hitched to it the four-steed team, he tied (the reins) at his side:
52“Slaughterer,” “Merciless,” “Overwhelmer,” “Soaring.”
53Their lips are curled back, their teeth bear venom,
54They know not fatigue, they are trained to trample down.
55He stationed at his right gruesome battle and strife,
56At his left fray that overthrows all formations.
57He was garbed in a ghastly armored garment,

translation.text:
58On his head he was covered with terrifying glories.
59The Lord made straight and pursued his way,
60Toward raging Tiamat he set his face.
61He was holding a magic spell ready upon his lips,
62A plant, antidote to venom, he was grasping in his hand.
63At that moment the gods were stirring, stirring about him,
64The gods his fathers were stirring about him, the gods stirring about him.
65The Lord drew near, to see the battle of Tiamat,
66He was looking for the stratagem of Qingu her spouse.
67As he looked, his advance turned to confusion,
68His thinking was disconcerted and his actions panicky,
69And as for the gods his allies, who went at his side,
70When they saw the valiant vanguard, their sight failed them.
71Tiamat cast her magic spell pointblank,
72Falsehood, lies she held ready on her lips.
73“… lord, the gods rise against you,
74“They assembled [where] they are, (but) are they on your side?”
75The Lord [raised] the Deluge, his great weapon,
76To Tiamat, who acted conciliatory, sent he (this word),
77“Why outwardly do you assume a friendly attitude,
78“While your heart is plotting to open attack?

translation.text:
84“And you have perpetrated your evil against the gods my fathers.
85“Though your main force is drawn up, though these your weapons are in array,
86“Come within range, let us meet in single combat, you and I!”
87When Tiamat heard this,
88She was beside herself, she turned into a maniac.
89Tiamat shrieked loud, in a passion,
90Her frame shook all over, down to the ground.
91She was reciting an incantation, casting her spell,
92While the gods of battle were whetting their blades.
93Tiamat and Marduk, sage of the gods, drew close,
94They locked in single combat, joining for the fray.
95The Lord spread out his net, encircled her,
96The ill wind he was holding behind him he released in her face.
97Tiamat opened her mouth to swallow (him),
98He thrust in the ill wind so she could not close her lips.
99The raging winds bloated her belly,
100Her insides were stopped up, she gaped her mouth wide.
101He shot off an arrow, it ruptured her belly,
102It cut to her innards, it pierced the heart.
103He subdued her and snuffed out her life,
104He flung down her carcass, he took a stand upon it.
105After he had slain Tiamat, the vanguard.
106Her forces scattered, her host dispersed.

translation.text:
107As for the gods her allies, who had marched beside her,
108In fear and trembling they turned tail,
109They tried to find a way out to save their lives,
110There was no escaping the mesh that encircled them.
111He drew them in and smashed their weapons.
112They were cast in the net and sat in a heap,
113They were heaped up in the corners, full of woe,
114They were bearing his punishment, held in confinement.
115As for the eleven creatures, the ones adorned with glories,
116The demonic horde(?), who went as flunkies at her side,
117He put on leadropes, he trussed their arms.
118He trampled them under, together with their belligerence.
119As for Qingu, who was trying to be great among them,
120He bound him and reckoned him among the doomed gods.
121He took away from him the tablet of destinies, which he had no right to,
122He sealed it with a seal and affixed it to his chest.
123Having captured his enemies and triumphed,
124Having shown the vaunted foe subservient(?),
125Having brought about Anshar's victory over all his enemies,
126Having attained what Nudimmud desired, young Marduk
127Made firm his hold over the captured gods,
128Then turned back to Tiamat whom he had rendered helpless.
129The Lord trampled upon the frame of Tiamat,

136That he might divide the brine and fashion artful things.
137He split her in two, like a fish for drying,
138Half of her he set up and made as a cover, heaven.
139He stretched out the hide, assigned watchmen,
140Them he ordered not to let her waters escape.
141He crossed heaven, he inspected the firmament,
142He made it a counterpart to Apsu, the dwelling of Nudimmud.
143The Lord measured the construction of Apsu,
144He founded the Great Sanctuary, the likeness of Esharra
145(In) the Great Sanctuary, the Esharra he had built, (and in) heaven,
146He made Ea, Enlil, and Anu dwell in their holy places.
